title: Listening, Speaking and Project Work

overview.intro: The theory paper is only part of English Core. Twenty marks are assessed internally by the school — listening for five, speaking for five and project work for ten — and the curriculum pairs them with an extended reading programme. This unit explains what each component assesses, how to listen actively rather than merely hear, how to speak so that an audience can follow, and how to plan, research, present and document a project that stands up to scrutiny.

learningOutcomes: Describe what each of the three components assesses.

blocks.text: The listening component assesses the ability to take in spoken material and work with it: to identify the main idea, to note supporting detail, to distinguish fact from opinion, and to retain structure after hearing the passage a limited number of times. The skill involved is active rather than passive — a listener is constantly predicting, checking and correcting, much as a reader does, except that the material disappears as it is delivered. Because there is no second chance to re-read a sentence, note-taking becomes part of listening itself rather than a separate activity.

Practical preparation has three parts. First, before the passage begins, use the questions to decide what kind of information you are hunting for — names, sequence, reason, contrast. Second, while listening, record in a compact shorthand: key nouns, numbers, connectives such as but, because and however (which carry the argument), and a mark for each new paragraph of thought. Third, after listening, spend the working time converting notes into answers immediately, because raw notes are only legible for a few minutes. Practice improves all three, and the single most effective drill is to listen to a short broadcast item and summarise it aloud in three sentences.

items: Listening assesses comprehension, detail and evaluation of spoken material.
Notes should hold nouns, numbers and connectives, not full sentences.
Connectives carry the argument: but, because, however, therefore.
Predict from the questions before the passage starts.
Summarise in three sentences while the material is still fresh.

learn.title: Speaking: being understood by an audience

blocks.text: Speaking is assessed on intelligibility, organisation and interaction rather than on accent or vocabulary. A good spoken performance has three properties: it can be followed by someone hearing it for the first time, it is organised so the listener always knows where they are, and it is delivered at a pace the ear can process. The commonest failures are rushing, beginning without stating the point, and ending without a close — all of which are correctable by preparation rather than by talent.

Preparation follows the same logic as writing but with different constraints. A short presentation needs one thesis sentence, three points in a defensible order, an example for each, and a closing sentence that signals the end — written on a card as keywords rather than a script, because reading aloud removes eye contact and flattens rhythm. For interaction, listening to the other speaker is itself assessed: answering the question actually asked, building on what was said, and disagreeing with reasons rather than volume. Pronunciation matters only insofar as it obstructs understanding, and the way to improve it is to record yourself and listen for the words you slurred rather than for the sound of your own voice.

learn.title: Project work: from topic to submission

blocks.text: Project work carries the largest share of the internal marks, and unlike speaking it can be prepared thoroughly in advance. Its stages are fixed even when its topics are free: choose a topic that can be researched with available sources rather than one that only opinion can address; collect material from more than one source and record full publication details as you go; organise notes under headings before writing anything; draft the project with an introduction that states the question, a body that answers it in sections, and a conclusion that states what the work established; and finally prepare a short presentation of the project for assessment or discussion.

Documentation is where marks are most often lost. Every quotation needs its source, every paraphrase needs attribution, and a bibliography in a consistent format signals that the work has provenance rather than borrowed certainty. The project should also reflect the student’s own organisation: headings, a logical sequence, legible presentation and, where useful, a table, chart or diagram that carries information more efficiently than prose. Assessment criteria generally reward relevance, research quality, structure and presentation — so before submitting, check the work against those four headings yourself, because self-assessment against the rubric is the cheapest available improvement.

blocks.text: Alongside the assessed components, the curriculum prescribes extended reading — substantial books read beyond the prescribed texts, usually recorded and discussed rather than examined in detail. Its purpose is to make the examined skills habitual: a student who reads regularly acquires vocabulary, sentence sense and the ability to follow an argument without the apparatus of questions. The practical method is modest but firm: a fixed time daily, a record of what was read with a line or two of comment, and periodic discussion so that reading becomes communicative rather than private.

The three components of the internal assessment reinforce each other, and this is worth understanding rather than memorising. Listening trains the ear that speaking must satisfy; speaking teaches the economy that writing also needs; projects develop research that the written answers of the theory paper implicitly assume. A student who practises one improves the others, which is the curriculum’s design rather than a coincidence. For examination purposes, the marks are what they are — five, five and ten — but the competence assessed is the same competence the theory paper rewards.

items: Extended reading builds vocabulary, sentence sense and sustained attention.
Record what was read with a line of comment; discuss periodically.
Listening trains the ear that speaking must satisfy.
Speaking teaches economy that writing also needs.
Projects develop research the theory paper assumes.

questions.prompt: What three skills does the internal assessment assess, and how are the marks distributed?
questions.answer: It assesses three skills for twenty marks in total: listening for five marks, where the student must follow spoken material, note detail and evaluate what was heard; speaking for five marks, where organisation, intelligibility and interaction are judged; and project work for ten marks, where a researched topic must be selected, investigated from recorded sources, organised and presented. The components are assessed internally by the school alongside the prescribed extended reading programme.
questions.explanation: All three components with their marks and a one-line description of each are required.

questions.prompt: Describe a reliable method for taking notes while listening.
questions.answer: The method has three phases. Before the passage, use the questions to decide what you are hunting for — a sequence, a reason, a comparison — so that the ear is directed rather than merely open. During the passage, record only compact items: key nouns, numbers, and the connectives (but, however, because, therefore) that signal how the argument is moving, marking each new stretch of thought so the structure survives in the notes. After the passage, convert those notes into answers immediately, since raw shorthand loses its meaning within minutes. The method should be practised on short broadcast items — listen once, then summarise in three sentences — because the constraint of disappearing material is what note-taking is designed to beat.
questions.explanation: Three phases with their specific content are required, plus the practice drill.

questions.prompt: Plan a project on a topic of your choice and explain how you would ensure its quality.
questions.answer: The topic is the transformation of a local street or marketplace over thirty years, chosen because sources exist: municipal records, newspapers, photographs and interviews are all obtainable locally, and the question is narrow enough to answer within a project’s length. The research stage begins with a source list and proceeds by recording full publication details as I go — for every quotation and every paraphrase — because provenance is what separates research from assertion, and a consistent bibliography is compiled alongside rather than after the writing. Organisation comes next: notes are sorted under headings (background, changes, causes, present condition) before drafting, so that the write-up follows a structure the material supports rather than one imposed on it. The document itself will open by stating the question, develop it in those sections with evidence and at least one table or chart carrying information that prose would bury, and close by stating what the work established rather than restating the question. The final stage is a short presentation with a stated thesis and a close, prepared from keywords rather than a script, followed by questions. Before submission I would check the work against the four headings the rubric rewards — relevance (does every section answer the question), research (is every claim sourced), structure (does the sequence follow the argument) and presentation (are headings, legibility and the bibliography in order) — since self-assessment against published criteria is the cheapest available improvement and the most commonly skipped.
questions.explanation: Full marks need all five stages in order, explicit provenance practice, the rubric check, and one justified choice of topic.

questions.prompt: “The internal assessment trains the same competencies the theory paper examines.” Discuss whether this is true of all three components.
questions.answer: The case for listening is strong and direct. The theory paper’s reading sections require comprehension of unseen passages under time pressure — identifying main ideas, extracting detail, evaluating tone — and these are exactly the operations the listening component demands of material that disappears as it is delivered. Note-taking during listening trains the same condensation that written answers require: reducing a passage to its argument and its evidence without copying it. Indeed listening is the harder version of the skill, because the reader of a passage may re-read and the listener may not; practised listeners arrive at reading comprehension already fluent in the economy the paper rewards. The case for speaking is more indirect but real. Answering in full sentences orally rehearses the shape the paper’s short answers must take — a direct response, supporting detail, and a close — and organising a talk teaches the same constraint the written answer imposes: one point per unit, in an order the audience can follow. Interaction in speaking, where a student must answer what was actually asked rather than what they had prepared, is precisely the discipline that prevents candidates in an examination from writing around a question they did not fully understand. The case for project work is the clearest of the three, because the paper’s longer answers are compressed projects: they require a reading of the question as a problem, an organisation of material under headings, evidence attached to each claim, and a conclusion that states what was established. Research skills transfer as the ability to marshal knowledge accurately rather than to recite it, and documentation habits transfer as precision about attribution and detail. The qualification worth adding is that none of the transfers is automatic: a student may speak fluently and still write badly if vocabulary and sentence control are not developed, and a beautifully presented project does not guarantee speed under examination conditions, where time pressure rather than knowledge is often the binding constraint. The balanced judgement is therefore that the components assess overlapping competencies and develop them under different conditions — the listening ear, the speaking structure and the researched project each train a facet of the same competence, while the paper adds the two conditions the classroom does not supply: time and writing at speed. Answers should illustrate each of the three transfers with a concrete parallel and then add the qualification, because the claim is substantially true but requires that condition to be stated honestly.
questions.explanation: Full marks require all three components analysed with a concrete parallel to a paper skill, plus the qualification about what does not transfer automatically.
